title: How the DNA Model Was Built

generated.pipeline: extract → Sonnet draft → Sonnet accuracy gate (separate agent) → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: A {{c1::model}} is a simplified representation that helps explain or predict something real.
cards.quote: A model is a simplified representation that helps explain or predict something real.

cards.front: A {{c1::nucleotide}} is one building block of DNA, made of a sugar, a phosphate group and a base.
cards.quote: A nucleotide is one building block of DNA, made of a sugar, a phosphate group and a base.

cards.front: DNA has four bases, written {{c1::A, T, G and C}}.
cards.quote: DNA has four bases, written A, T, G and C.

cards.front: A city map is a good analogy for a DNA model. What is the limit of that analogy?
cards.back: A map is drawn from a place you can visit. The B-form double helix is about 2 nanometers wide, too narrow to see, so its models had to be built from measurements.
cards.quote: The B-form double helix is about 2 nanometers wide, far too narrow to see with your eyes or a light microscope.

cards.front: A student wants to show how DNA is packed into a cell. Which view fits, and what does it hide?
cards.back: The chromosome view, which shows large-scale packing. It hides the individual base pairs.
cards.quote: The chromosome view shows large-scale packing. It hides the individual base pairs.
cards.section: Explore: four models of one molecule

cards.front: You want to compare one gene in your DNA with the same gene in a classmate's. Which model do you choose, and what do you lose by choosing it?
cards.back: The base-letter string, because it shows the order of bases for comparing. You lose the shape, the size and the partner strand.
cards.why: Rule: choose a DNA model by the question; every model leaves features out.
cards.quote: Then decide which model best compares one gene with a classmate's.
cards.section: Explore: four models of one molecule

cards.front: A student wants to see how much space the atoms of DNA fill and how the molecule's outside looks. Which model fits, and what might it hide?
cards.back: A space-filling model, with atoms drawn as balls. It can hide the base pairs inside the molecule.
cards.why: Rule: every model leaves features out.
cards.quote: The one idea: Choose DNA models by the question; every model leaves features out.
cards.section: Explore: four models of one molecule

cards.front: If every DNA model leaves features out, does that make all models equally accurate?
cards.back: No. The rule applies to every model, but evidence can rule a model out.
cards.quote: It does not make all models equally accurate; evidence can rule a model out.
cards.section: Explore: four models of one molecule

cards.front: Which three kinds of evidence was the 1953 double helix model built to fit?
cards.back: Base-amount data, X-ray measurements and chemistry (what the parts are and how they fit together).
cards.quote: The double helix model was built to fit base-amount data, X-ray measurements and chemistry together, and later tests supported it.
cards.section: Three kinds of evidence, one model

cards.front: In base pairing, A pairs with {{c1::T}} and G pairs with C across the two strands.
cards.quote: Base pairing, the rule that A pairs with T and G pairs with C across the two strands, explained the equal amounts of A and T.
cards.section: Three kinds of evidence, one model

cards.front: X-rays were scattered from lined-up DNA fibers into spots. What did the spacing of the spots point to, and what did it not give?
cards.back: It pointed to a helix about 2 nanometers wide and gave repeat distances. It was not a photograph of the bases.
cards.quote: Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling measured diffraction patterns, including one often called Photo 51.
cards.section: Three kinds of evidence, one model

cards.front: What fiber evidence, and what chemistry, supported putting the phosphate backbones on the outside of the double helix?
cards.back: DNA fibers changed as the air got wetter or drier, which fits phosphates facing water. The charged phosphate backbones had to face the surrounding water.
cards.quote: Their work on how DNA fibers changed as the air got wetter or drier also supported the idea that the phosphates sit on the outside, facing water.
cards.section: Three kinds of evidence, one model

cards.front: A species has more G and C than A and T. Does that rule out base pairing in the double helix?
cards.back: No. Pairing predicts only that G is close to C and A is close to T, not that all four bases are equal.
cards.why: The base mix differs among species.
cards.quote: No. Pairing predicts only that G is close to C and A is close to T.
cards.section: Three kinds of evidence, one model

cards.front: Describe the double helix model published on 25 April 1953.
cards.back: Two strands of DNA coiled around each other, running in opposite directions, with the backbones outside and the bases inside.
cards.quote: Their model, published on 25 April 1953, was the double helix: two strands of DNA coiled around each other, running in opposite directions, with the backbones outside and bases inside.
cards.section: Three kinds of evidence, one model

cards.front: Why did base pairing suggest how DNA could be copied?
cards.back: Each strand fixes the order of its partner, so one strand can serve as the guide for a new partner.
cards.quote: It also suggested how DNA could be copied, because each strand fixes the order of its partner.
cards.section: Three kinds of evidence, one model

cards.front: The double helix shows DNA's shape. What did sequencing add?
cards.back: The letters, how many there are, and how they differ between people.
cards.quote: Sequencing added the letters, how many there are, and how they differ between people.

cards.front: In Sanger sequencing, how do stop blocks let scientists read the base order?
cards.back: A small amount of stop blocks mixed in with ordinary ones stops copies at many different matching positions. Sorted by length, the copies reveal the base order of the new strand.
cards.quote: Its core trick: a small amount of stop blocks, mixed in with ordinary ones, stops copies at many different matching positions.

cards.front: In the 1977 method, four reactions each held a stop block for only one kind of base. A copy came from the reaction with the C stop block. What does that tell you?
cards.back: The copy ended with a C stop block, so the new strand's last base in that copy is C. The reaction a copy came from tells which base ended it.
cards.quote: So the reaction a copy came from told which base ended it.

cards.front: One strand reads TTAGC. What does its partner read when each partner base is written directly underneath?
cards.back: AATCG. T pairs with A, A with T, G with C and C with G.
cards.quote: G pairs with C, A with T, T with A and C with G.

cards.front: A {{c1::genome}} is all the DNA in one set of an organism's chromosomes.
cards.quote: A genome is all the DNA in one set of an organism's chromosomes, and a chromosome is one long DNA molecule wound with proteins.

cards.front: A human genome has about {{c1::3 billion}} base pairs.
cards.quote: A human genome has about 3 billion base pairs.

cards.front: What was the Human Genome Project (October 1990 to April 2003), and what did it produce?
cards.back: An international project that read the order of bases in human DNA, mostly with improved Sanger sequencing. It produced a reference sequence used for comparison.
cards.quote: It mostly used improved Sanger sequencing and produced a reference sequence, a standard human DNA sequence used for comparison.

cards.front: Was the human reference sequence the DNA of one single person, and was it complete?
cards.back: No. It was pieced together from several donors, with about 70 percent from one donor, and it still had gaps.
cards.quote: It was pieced together from several donors, with about 70 percent from one donor, and it still had gaps.

cards.front: Sequencers read short pieces that a computer joins by overlaps. Why would longer reads help fill gaps around repeated stretches?
cards.back: Repeated stretches make joining overlapping pieces hard; if longer pieces can span the repeat, they avoid wrong joins. The lesson says this is one reason long-read methods helped fill gaps in 2022.
cards.why: Rests on: a computer joins overlapping pieces, and repeats make this hard.
cards.quote: This is one reason long-read methods helped fill gaps in 2022.

cards.front: Later measurements refined details of the double helix model. Did they overturn it?
cards.back: No. The main features still hold. Details such as how many base pairs make one turn were refined.
cards.quote: The main features of the double helix model still hold, though later measurements refined details such as how many base pairs make one turn.

cards.front: NHGRI's estimated cost per human-sized genome was $3,063,820 in January 2008 and $46,774 in January 2010. About how many times cheaper was January 2010?
cards.back: About 65 times cheaper. 3,063,820 divided by 46,774 is about 65.5. From 606 dollars in 2019 to 525 dollars in 2022 is a far smaller change.
cards.quote: The recent change is much smaller: 606 to 525 dollars, against a fall of about 65 times from 2008 to 2010.
cards.section: The falling cost of a genome

cards.front: NHGRI estimated $95,263,072 per human-sized genome in September 2001 and $525 in May 2022. About how many times cheaper is that?
cards.back: Roughly 180,000 times cheaper. 95,263,072 divided by 525 is about 181,500.
cards.quote: Newer technology plus a reference cut NHGRI's estimate from about 95 million dollars in 2001 to about 525 dollars in 2022.

cards.front: Why should the early and late NHGRI cost estimates not be compared as if they price the same job?
cards.back: Early values cover Sanger sequencing read enough times to build a genome without a reference. Later values cover short reads lined up against the human reference, which needs less reading. They price somewhat different jobs.
cards.quote: NHGRI notes that a genome without a reference would need more reading, so the early and late estimates price somewhat different jobs.
cards.section: The falling cost of a genome

cards.front: Design a paper-strip test of whether longer pieces make it easier to rebuild a sequence containing a repeat. What are the independent and dependent variables?
cards.back: Use a 60-letter made-up sequence with the same 8-letter stretch twice, cut into overlapping strips. Independent variable: strip length (such as 6, 12 and 20 letters). Dependent variable: whether a classmate rebuilds it correctly, and how long it takes. Keep the sequence, number of copies and random cuts constant.
cards.quote: Sequencing machines read short pieces of DNA, and a computer joins overlapping pieces back together.
